title: levenshtein_less_equal clamps stop_column only from above, so an overflowed cost product drives an out-of-bounds write into the palloc'd row
live_proof: upstream c4d51b6274, "Avoid overflow in Levenshtein distance calculations", which postdates the 17.5 pin. Upstream states it plainly: the SQL functions accept any 32-bit integer for each cost, the distances are computed in 32-bit arithmetic, and "certain inputs to levenshtein_less_equal() can even cause out-of-bounds writes". Five lines of src/backend/utils/adt/levenshtein.c carry it at the pin. :152 -- `min_theo_d = net_inserts < 0 ? -net_inserts * del_c : net_inserts * ins_c;` multiplies two ints into an int, which overflows for large caller-supplied costs. :175 -- `int slack_d = max_d - min_theo_d;` inherits the wrong value. :178 -- `stop_column = best_column + (slack_d / (ins_c + del_c)) + 1;`. :179-180 -- `if (stop_column > m) stop_column = m + 1;` clamps ONLY FROM ABOVE, so a stop_column that came out negative or otherwise below range passes through untouched. :212 -- `prev = (int *) palloc(2 * m * sizeof(int));`. :240 -- `prev[stop_column] = max_d + 1;` writes at that index. Upstream widens the whole computation to int64 and replaces the one-sided clamp with `stop_column = Min(tmp, m + 1)`.
fidelity: real server, core arithmetic reached through contrib/fuzzystrmatch. The write is into a palloc'd chunk; how far out of range it lands depends on the costs supplied, which is caller-controlled, so this case can probe both inside and outside the aset block from the same code path. Trigger derived and then verified, in that order. The first version used round numbers (2000000000, 1073741824) and reached nothing: every one of them tripped the early `if (min_theo_d > max_d) return max_d + 1` and left the function before stop_column was computed at all. Modelling the three int32 operations instead gives a parameter set that drives stop_column to -1: source 3 characters, target 200, ins_c 715827883, del_c 1, max_d 2000000000. 197 * 715827883 overflows negative, slack_d then overflows in turn, and the clamp at :179 is one-sided so -1 passes through to prev[-1]. On a native 17.5 cluster on 2026-10-06 this returns -715827814: a Levenshtein distance cannot be negative, so the return value is itself evidence that the overflow occurred and was used. The server does not crash, as expected -- prev[-1] lands inside the palloc chunk's own block.
